Why 'Lensatic'?

For anyone handed a framework, a maturity model, or a zero trust deadline and asked where it fits: federal civilian agencies, DoW components, defense contractors, and anyone else borrowing the United States federal models. Start at the trailhead that describes you.
Zero trust, the idea most of these documents serve, means nothing is trusted because of where it connects from: every request to reach data or a system is checked against policy each time.
Pick the trailhead that describes you. Steps run in the order you do them; the layer tag on each step shows where it sits on the stack below.
Federal civilian agency
You run or build systems for a federal civilian agency, and you have been told to do zero trust.
Start with Executive Order (EO) 14028, section 3, which orders the move to zero trust architecture and sets the outcome for every civilian agency.

Read the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) memorandum M-22-09 for the specific goals every agency must meet, due by the end of fiscal year 2024 and still binding, organized by the five pillars of the maturity model from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).
Use National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publication (SP) 800-207 for what zero trust means, so the program is an architecture and not a product list.
Place yourself on the CISA maturity model's four stages, pillar by pillar; the memo's goals are the floor, and the next stage is the plan.
Select and tailor SP 800-53 controls through the Risk Management Framework (RMF), so the target maps to controls your assessors test and your authorizing official signs.
Express the target as a Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 Profile, which EO 13800 already directs your agency to use, so leadership can fund it in outcome language.
Assess the controls against SP 800-53A, obtain and keep the authorization under the RMF, and keep current the zero trust implementation plan the memo had you file with OMB and CISA.
DoW component
You are a DoW component, or a program that reports to one, working toward Target Level zero trust.

Start with the DoD Zero Trust Strategy and its execution roadmap, which set the Target Level, the deadline, and the phasing; the implementing memorandum, directive-type memorandum (DTM) 25-003, passed its printed expiry on 17 July 2026 with no replacement found, so the FY2027 deadline rests on those two documents. Keep your component's zero trust implementation plan current and ask the zero trust portfolio office what it expects now: the strategy set the first plans due to the DoW CIO and JFHQ-DODIN, now the Cyber Defense Command, by 23 September 2023, and no current source repeats the yearly submission the DTM required.

Work the seven pillars and 45 capabilities as your model; each capability breaks into activities, 152 in all, and the 91 at Target Level come first, with the 61 at Advanced Level where the mission needs them; the roadmap offers three courses of action (uplift your own infrastructure, use a commercial cloud, or use an on-premises cloud the department or a component owns) and lets you mix them, and an enterprise service can deliver some activities for you (see Questions).

If you own control systems or other operational technology, work its zero trust activities and outcomes alongside the enterprise ones; they add to your existing cybersecurity requirements, and the document says separate guidance will be developed for weapon systems and defense critical infrastructure.
Use the National Security Agency (NSA) information sheets for each pillar and the 2026 implementation guidelines to sequence the activities.

Apply the DoD Zero Trust Overlays to select the SP 800-53 controls that implement each capability; the overlays are not posted publicly in 2026, so ask your component or the zero trust portfolio office for the current copy.

Show proof of each Target Level outcome to your authorizing official and the DoW CIO zero trust portfolio office, keep the Risk Management Framework (RMF) authorization current, and expect the Cyber Operational Readiness Assessment (CORA) to assess the readiness of the defended network; a system that cannot meet Target Level needs a waiver request to the portfolio office, renewed every year, for the CIO's approval.
Express the target as a Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 Profile, which Executive Order (EO) 13800 directs every agency head to use, so leadership sees the program in outcome language.
Defense contractor handling controlled unclassified information (CUI)
You are a contractor or subcontractor that handles controlled unclassified information for a DoW customer.

If you hold only federal contract information, the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) basic safeguarding clause, 52.204-21 (52.240-93 in contracts written under the FAR overhaul deviations), sets your 15 requirements; if you hold controlled unclassified information for a civilian agency, that agency's own contract clauses name the requirements; the Everyone else trailhead covers both cases.

Start with Special Publication (SP) 800-171 Revision 2 from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), the 110 requirements that Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (DFARS) clause 252.204-7012 and its class deviation make you meet for controlled unclassified information; Revision 3 is NIST's current edition and applies only when a contract says so.

Know your Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) level from the contract's 252.204-7021 clause: Phase 1 self-assessments against SP 800-171 Revision 2 still run, and the certified-assessment phases are suspended as of July 2026. Two duties never paused: DFARS 252.204-7012, which also has you report cyber incidents, and the DFARS 252.204-7019 provision, which asks for a current SP 800-171 self-assessment score in the Supplier Performance Risk System (SPRS).

Use SP 800-207 for what zero trust means. No rule at this trailhead requires it of you; the DoD Zero Trust Strategy expects the Defense Industrial Base to execute it, and it reaches you through what a customer writes into a contract.
Borrow whichever model your customer uses, the DoW seven pillars or the CISA maturity model, so your target state speaks their language; for a DoW customer that is the seven-pillar view.
Use the Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 to tell leadership and customers where you are and where you are going.
Everyone else
You are a company, a state or local government, a university, or anyone else with no federal mandate to meet.
Nothing on this stack binds you by its own force; a government contract can, and the two cases below say how.

Use the Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to say what good looks like, NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-207 to define zero trust, the zero trust maturity model of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to set a target (its four stages are public and written to be borrowed), and SP 800-53, or a smaller catalog such as the Center for Internet Security (CIS) Controls, for controls. If a customer or regulator names a framework, start from that one and work up and down the stack from there. Verification is whoever checks your evidence: an internal audit, a certifier, or a customer assessment; the layer 5 entries here are federal. If you hold federal contract information or controlled unclassified information for a government customer, the two cases below say what applies; if you hold controlled unclassified information under a DoW contract, start at the contractor trailhead.
Federal contract information only

Federal contract information is information not intended for public release that is provided by or generated for the government under a contract. If you hold only federal contract information for any agency, the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) basic safeguarding clause, 52.204-21 (52.240-93 in contracts written under the FAR overhaul deviations), sets your 15 requirements, and on a DoW contract that carries the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) clause, Level 1 is a self-assessment against those same 15. Nothing else on this stack binds you; use CSF 2.0 to talk about the rest.
Controlled unclassified information for a civilian agency

Controlled unclassified information is government information that is not classified but that a law, regulation or government-wide policy requires or permits agencies to safeguard or control. If you hold controlled unclassified information for a civilian agency, your contract clause names the requirements, normally a revision of SP 800-171, and the assessment the clause specifies proves them; CMMC does not apply. Use SP 800-207 for what zero trust means, the CISA maturity model if the agency asks for a target, and CSF 2.0 to tell the agency where you stand.
SP 800-207 defines zero trust architecture: no implicit trust from network location, and every request decided by a policy engine and then allowed or blocked at a policy enforcement point.
CSF 2.0 gives an organization six functions, Profiles, and Tiers to describe cybersecurity outcomes in language leadership funds against.
SP 800-53 is the catalog of security and privacy controls that federal systems select from, and that CSF references and the zero trust overlays both point into.
The AI RMF gives an organization four functions, Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage, to handle the risks of AI systems in outcome language.

The Cyber AI Profile is a draft CSF 2.0 Community Profile that crosses the six functions with three focus areas: securing AI system components, conducting AI-enabled cyber defense, and thwarting AI-enabled cyber attacks.
The AI Defense Matrix lays the six CSF 2.0 functions across eight AI-specific asset classes, from models and training data to agent identities, the same two-axis move the zero trust matrix makes.

Policy names who may access what, under which conditions, and who owns the identity rules the policy engine enforces. Identity risk is part of the enterprise risk strategy.
An inventory of users, roles, and privileges, including service and non-person accounts, kept current. Identity risk signals feed access decisions.
Phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication for people, certificate or managed identities for non-person accounts, least privilege, and a per-request access decision for every account.

User and privileged-account activity is baselined and analyzed for anomalies, and identity risk is scored continuously so that a session can be challenged or ended mid-flight, not only at the next sign-in.
Credentials and sessions are revoked or stepped down at once when an incident touches an identity, and the policy engine tightens access automatically.
After an incident, compromised credentials are rotated, standing privileges are re-approved rather than restored wholesale, and affected users are told what changed as their access is re-enabled.
Policy sets what a device must prove before it may connect, and a named owner holds device trust, including trust in the hardware and software supply chain.
An inventory of every device, managed or not, with an owner, a posture, and a risk rating.
Device posture (patch level, configuration, health) is checked before and during access, and access is denied or limited when posture fails.

Every device that connects is detected and has its compliance confirmed, endpoint telemetry feeds detection and response tooling, and a device that drifts out of posture surfaces as an event and is reflected in its next access decision.
A compromised device is isolated automatically and its access is cut off while the incident is handled.

A rebuilt or restored device re-enrolls, re-attests its configuration and patch state, and passes the compliance check again before it regains any access, and the restoration is confirmed to the people who depend on it.
Policy covers how applications and workloads authenticate, authorize, and are approved for use, and trust in the software supply chain is a governance concern.
An inventory of applications, workloads, interfaces, and their data flows, with owners and risk ratings.
Every application call is authenticated and authorized, workloads run with least privilege, and secure development and deployment practices are enforced.

Applications and workloads are monitored continuously, which keeps their authorization to operate current, and are checked against their profile and behavior baselines; unexpected calls or state changes are correlated with identity and device telemetry to characterize the event.

A misbehaving workload is isolated at its enforcement point, its service credentials and tokens are revoked so the policy engine denies its calls, and its state is captured for analysis before it is stopped or torn down.

Workloads are redeployed from a verified, known-good build through the normal pipeline rather than patched in place, and their authorization is re-established. Application owners are told when the redeployed workload is back in service, and what was learned changes the deployment checks.
Policy defines data categories, handling rules, and who owns each data set, and data risk is part of the enterprise risk strategy.
Data is inventoried, labeled and tagged, and the risk to each category is assessed.
Data is encrypted at rest and in transit, access is granted per request based on the data's label, and loss prevention controls apply.

Access, sharing, transformation, and use of data are captured as active metadata in every state, loss-prevention sensing flags exfiltration attempts, and unusual access patterns are analyzed against the data's label and its normal use.
Access to affected data is restricted at once, and the exposure is analyzed and reported to the people who must know.
Data is restored from backups whose integrity is verified first, restored records keep their labels and access rules, and the owners and any external parties are told what was restored and when.
Policy replaces location with identity and context as the basis for access, and a named owner holds the segmentation and network access rules.
Network flows, segments, and dependencies are mapped, and the risk of each path is assessed.
The network is segmented, traffic is encrypted, and each connection is authorized rather than trusted because of where it starts.
All traffic, including traffic inside the perimeter, is logged and analyzed, decrypted for inspection only where policy allows, and unusual flows are characterized and correlated across sources.
Segments and paths are closed or re-routed quickly to contain an incident.

Segments and paths closed during containment are reopened in priority order as their integrity is confirmed, and resilience configurations absorb the shifted load. Normal traffic patterns are verified against the flow map before trust is widened, and the reopening order is reported to the mission owners who depend on each path.
Policy sets which decisions may be automated and which need a human, and names who owns the orchestration of policy changes.
Automated runbooks and the systems they touch are inventoried, and the risk of automated action is assessed.
Access decisions are made and enforced by machine at the speed of each request, and configuration is enforced through automation rather than by hand.
Detection rules run automatically across the telemetry, and alerts are triaged by machine before a human sees them.
Containment, policy change, and notification are orchestrated automatically, with a human in the loop where policy requires one.

Recovery runbooks execute the restoration steps that can be automated in a set order, and the orchestrator's step log is what the recovery status reported to stakeholders is drawn from. The runbooks are revised from the incident before the next use.
Policy requires that every access decision and control produce telemetry, and oversight uses that telemetry to check whether the program works.
Telemetry sources are inventoried, and gaps in visibility are treated as risks to close.

Log records are generated for every access decision and made available for monitoring, logs and telemetry are protected as data in their own right, and analytics results feed the policy engine's access decisions.

Telemetry from users, devices, networks, applications, and data is collected in one security information and event management (SIEM) platform, enriched with threat intelligence, and correlated across pillars continuously, so activity that looks normal in one pillar and abnormal across several surfaces as an event.

Retained logs and analytics let responders establish what happened and its root cause, incident data is collected with its integrity and provenance preserved, and telemetry confirms that containment worked.

Telemetry confirms that restored assets behave as their baselines predict before recovery is declared complete, and recovery progress is reported from the telemetry rather than from estimates. The incident's timeline, assembled from the logs, is what the lessons-learned review works from.

Zero trust for agents is layers 2 and 3 applied to a new subject: an agent is a non-person entity, which SP 800-207 and the user pillar already cover. The AI RMF is the outcome layer for AI risk; the Cyber AI Profile applies the six functions to AI across its three focus areas; the AI Defense Matrix covers securing AI systems, the Profile's first focus area, not AI-enabled defense. CoSAI applies SP 800-207's policy decision point to agents: authorization stays outside the model, and each tool call gets its own access decision. The SOC Profile is a worked example of one Target Profile for an AI-enabled security operations center, one outcome per function. AI as the defender's tool lands in the automation pillar, where the DoW model names it and the CISA model leaves it out. None of the four frameworks in this column, nor the quick-start guide beside them, binds anyone by its own force; the instrument that governs federal agencies' use of AI, OMB Memorandum M-25-21 of 3 April 2025, is listed here as governance outside the cybersecurity stack, and it names none of them.
Govern
Written policy on what AI agents may do autonomously and where a human decides; a named owner for AI use in security operations. Humans in the Lead, in writing.
Identify
Inventory of AI models, agents, tools, and the data they can reach, treated as assets with owners and risk ratings.
Protect
Agents hold their own identities with least privilege; tool and data access bounded; prompts and outputs treated as untrusted input at boundaries.
Detect
Agent actions logged and monitored like any privileged account; anomalous tool use surfaces as an event.
Respond
Documented stop, contain, and roll-back procedure for a misbehaving agent, rehearsed like any incident playbook.
Recover
Restore from known-good configurations and models; lessons learned feed the Govern policy.
Is CSF 2.0 mandatory?

Not by its own force. CSF 2.0 is voluntary by design, and Executive Order 13800 makes each federal agency head, civilian and DoW, use it. For federal agencies the mandatory engine underneath is the RMF and SP 800-53 under FISMA, so the CSF is the communication and prioritization layer above the controls. Its Informative References map each outcome down to the controls.
How does CSF 2.0 differ from ISO/IEC 27001?

CSF 2.0 is an outcomes framework; ISO/IEC 27001 is a certifiable management system standard. They are complementary: an organization can hold an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate and still use a CSF Profile to talk about outcomes, and the Informative References cross-map the two. NIST's Informative Reference Catalog lists an ISO/IEC 27001:2022 to CSF 2.0 reference.
What do we do first?

If a mandate binds you, your trailhead's first step names it, and the trailhead's later steps supply the target. In CSF 2.0 terms: scope the Profile and gather what you need, then start with the Govern outcomes: organizational context, risk strategy, and roles. Build a Current Profile and a Target Profile, analyze the gaps and plan, then implement and update. The action plan comes from the gap between the two Profiles.
How does CSF 2.0 relate to zero trust?

SP 800-207 defines zero trust, and the zero trust models supply the pillars and the maturity ladder. CSF 2.0 does not define zero trust; it gives you the outcome language. Put your model's pillars as columns and the six functions as rows, fill the matrix, and the result is a zero trust Target Profile: leadership reads it in outcome language, and the Informative References under the Subcategories of each cell's Categories carry it down to SP 800-53 or your own control catalog. It also puts zero trust in Govern, Identify, and Detect, not only in Protect. Maturity stays with the zero trust model you use; CSF 2.0 Tiers characterize the rigor of an organization's cybersecurity risk governance and management practices.
Where are the mappings?

On the NIST site: the CSF 2.0 Reference Tool and the Informative Reference Catalog map each Subcategory to SP 800-53 and other sources. For either pillar model, each matrix cell carries CSF 2.0 categories; the Subcategories under those categories carry the Informative References to SP 800-53; the CISA model prints no control mapping of its own. For the DoW pillars, the DoD Zero Trust Overlays map each capability to SP 800-53 controls; they are not posted publicly in 2026, so a DoW component asks its own leadership or the zero trust portfolio office for the current copy, and anyone borrowing the pillars works from the capability list and the catalog. NIST's practice guide on implementing a zero trust architecture, SP 1800-35 (final, June 2025), also publishes mappings of zero trust architecture principles and technologies to commonly used security standards and guidelines; they map its example builds, not the CISA or DoW pillar models.
Where do SP 800-171, CMMC, FedRAMP, ISO/IEC 27001, CIS Controls, STIGs, IL4 through IL6, and MITRE ATT&CK land?

SP 800-171 and CMMC are the contractor trailhead: a requirements baseline and the assessment that proves it, layers 4 and 5. FedRAMP is the governmentwide program that certifies cloud services for agency use, so it is verification (layer 5); its Rev5 path assesses an SP 800-53 baseline (layer 4), and its 20x path, widely available since June 2026, assesses Key Security Indicators instead. ISO/IEC 27001 sits beside CSF 2.0 as a management system standard. CIS Controls are a control catalog, layer 4. STIGs and SRGs are the DoW configuration baseline at layer 4. IL4 through IL6 are DoW cloud impact levels that set the baseline and the authorization bar, layers 4 and 5 again. ATT&CK is not a layer: it is the map of adversary behavior the stack defends against, most useful under Detect and Respond, and CORA scores against its tactics.
Where do validated solutions and enterprise services land?

They are not frameworks. A solution such as Thunderdome or Flank Speed is an implementation vehicle measured against the layer 3 activities: an assessment tests which of the DoW zero trust activities the service delivers. An organization that adopts one may inherit some of those activities, not all of them (inherit is this app's word: the DoW activities table splits each activity between enterprise and component responsibility instead), and the way to say which are inherited and which are its own is an activity-level instrument: a record, activity by activity, of what the solution delivers and what the organization still does.
Where does operational technology land, and where does IEC 62443 fit?

Operational technology (OT) lands at layer 3. On the DoW side it has its own baseline: activities and outcomes that adapt the enterprise zero trust activities to OT and control systems under the same seven pillars, stay aligned with the enterprise IT activities, and are implemented in addition to existing cybersecurity requirements; the document says separate guidance will be developed for weapon systems and defense critical infrastructure. Civilian agencies have no separate OT baseline on this stack: the CISA maturity model is still their model, CISA's 2026 companion, Adapting Zero Trust Principles to Operational Technology, applies it to OT, and NIST SP 800-82 Revision 3 is NIST's guide to OT security. IEC 62443, from the International Electrotechnical Commission, is a series of standards for the security of industrial automation and control systems, not a zero trust model: the DoW document names it, with the Purdue Model, among the established reference architectures it treats as authoritative for classifying OT systems.
